When pytest is invoked with --debug on a Windows system using a non-UTF-8 default encoding, and test node IDs include characters outside the system codepage, no encoding error is raised.
When pytest is invoked with --debug using only ASCII test names, the debug log output is identical to the output produced before this change.
When the towncrier draft script is executed and changelog fragments contain non-ASCII text, the draft file is written successfully without encoding errors.
When LsofFdLeakChecker runs on a system with a non-UTF-8 locale, subprocess stdout is decoded using the system's preferred encoding without errors.

task_17.title: Add --config-file as a long-form alias for the -c CLI flag
task_17.description: The existing -c CLI flag, used to specify a custom configuration file, now also accepts --config-file as a long-form alias. This improves discoverability and clarity for users who may not immediately recognize the short -c flag's purpose. The change aligns pytest with conventions used by other Python tools such as mypy (--config-file) and black (--config). The help text and metavar were also updated for consistency.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: The pytest CLI only exposes a single-character -c flag for specifying a custom configuration file. This is not self-documenting and requires users—especially those new to a project—to consult the documentation to understand its meaning. Ensure that a descriptive long-form --config-file flag is available as an equivalent alias for -c, so users can specify a custom configuration file with either flag interchangeably.

expectation.grounded: The pytest CLI parser should register --config-file as an additional long-form option alongside the existing -c short option. Both flags must share the same destination (inifilename), accept a string argument, and behave identically—loading configuration from the specified file instead of auto-discovering implicit configuration files. The help output should reflect the new flag name and use an uppercase FILE metavar.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to invoke pytest with either -c <file> or --config-file <file> to load a custom configuration file. Both forms must produce the same behavior. The --config-file flag should appear in the CLI help output with a clear description of its purpose.

constraints.grounded: The existing -c flag must continue to work exactly as before—no change in destination, type, or semantics. The --config-file flag must not introduce a separate configuration path or override mechanism; it must be a pure alias sharing the same argument parser entry. The help text must not reference removed or renamed options.
constraints.conceptual: Backward compatibility with the existing -c flag must be fully preserved. Users relying on -c in scripts, CI configurations, or documentation must not be affected. The new flag must not alter configuration resolution logic or precedence.

behavior: Running pytest --config-file <path> loads the configuration file at <path>, identical to running pytest -c <path>.
The --config-file flag appears in pytest --help output under the general options group with a description indicating it loads configuration from a specified file.
The metavar displayed in help output for both -c and --config-file is FILE (uppercase).
Specifying both -c and --config-file simultaneously follows standard argparse behavior for aliases sharing a single destination (last value wins or treated as the same option).
The -c short flag continues to function unchanged for all existing use cases.
acceptance_criteria: When a user runs pytest --config-file pyproject.toml, pytest loads configuration from pyproject.toml exactly as it would with pytest -c pyproject.toml.
When a user runs pytest --help, the output shows --config-file as an available option alongside -c, with a help string describing its purpose.
When a user runs pytest -c pyproject.toml (existing short flag), behavior is identical to previous versions with no regressions.
When a user runs pytest --config-file with a nonexistent file, the error behavior matches that of pytest -c with a nonexistent file.
When a user inspects the CLI help, the metavar for the config file option is displayed as FILE.

task_16.title: caplog.set_level() clarifies threshold semantics and overrides logging.disable()
task_16.description: Previously, caplog.set_level() documentation ambiguously stated it 'sets the level of a logger', without clarifying it acts as a capture threshold. Additionally, if logging was globally disabled via logging.disable(), caplog.set_level() could not capture at the requested level. This update clarifies the threshold semantics in the docstring and introduces behavior where set_level() automatically re-enables the requested logging level when it has been suppressed by a prior logging.disable() call, ensuring caplog can capture messages at and above the specified threshold regardless of global disable state.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that caplog.set_level() clearly communicates it sets a capture threshold (not an exact level) and that it functions correctly even when logging has been globally disabled via logging.disable(). Previously, users had no indication that set_level() filters messages below the given severity, and caplog could silently fail to capture logs when logging.disable() had been called at a high level.

expectation.grounded: When caplog.set_level(level, logger) is called, the LogCaptureFixture must: (1) set the threshold on the specified logger (or root logger if none given) so that only messages at or above the specified severity are captured, (2) detect whether the requested level is currently suppressed by logging.disable() via logger.isEnabledFor(), and if so, call logging.disable() with a value just below the requested level (level - 10, floored at logging.NOTSET) to re-enable capture at that level and above, (3) handle both integer and string level arguments—valid string levels are translated via logging.getLevelName(); invalid string levels cause all logging to be re-enabled by calling logging.disable(logging.NOTSET), (4) preserve the original manager.disable value so it can be restored when the test ends. The _force_enable_logging method on LogCaptureFixture encapsulates this override logic and returns the original disabled level as an int.
expectation.conceptual: When a user sets the caplog capture level, the fixture should treat the specified level as a minimum severity threshold—messages below that severity are not captured. If global logging suppression (via logging.disable()) would prevent capture at the requested level, the fixture should automatically override the suppression to enable capture at that level and above. After the test completes, the original logging suppression state should be restored.

constraints.grounded: The override must not enable logging levels below the requested threshold; only levels at or above the requested level should be re-enabled. The original logging.disable() level (stored from logger.manager.disable) must be restored after the test to avoid side effects on subsequent tests. When a non-standard or invalid level string is provided, the fallback must re-enable all logging (logging.disable(logging.NOTSET)) rather than raising an error. Existing behavior for tests that do not use logging.disable() must not change.
constraints.conceptual: The logging override must be scoped to the duration of the test and must not leak state to other tests. Only the minimum necessary logging levels should be re-enabled—levels below the requested threshold should remain suppressed. Invalid level inputs should be handled gracefully without errors, defaulting to enabling all logging.

behavior: caplog.set_level(level) now sets a threshold: only log messages at or above the specified severity level are captured; messages below are excluded.

If logging.disable() was previously called with a level that would suppress the requested capture level, set_level() automatically lowers the global disable threshold to one step below the requested level, re-enabling capture.
When set_level() receives a valid string level name (e.g., 'DEBUG', 'WARNING'), it is translated to the corresponding integer level for the disable override check.
When set_level() receives an invalid or non-standard string level name that cannot be translated to an integer, all logging is re-enabled by setting the global disable level to NOTSET.
The original global disable level is preserved before any override and restored at the end of the test, ensuring no cross-test side effects.
The docstring for set_level() now explicitly states it sets a threshold and that messages less severe than the given level will not be captured.
acceptance_criteria: When caplog.set_level(logging.WARNING) is called, messages at WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL levels should be captured, while DEBUG and INFO messages should not appear in caplog.records.

When logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) has been called before a test, and the test calls caplog.set_level(logging.DEBUG), caplog should successfully capture DEBUG-level and above messages despite the prior global disable.
When logging.disable(logging.WARNING) has been called and caplog.set_level(logging.ERROR) is used, only ERROR and CRITICAL messages should be captured; WARNING and below should remain suppressed.
When caplog.set_level() is called with an invalid string level (not in logging._nameToLevel), all logging levels should be re-enabled for capture without raising an exception.
After a test that triggered the logging.disable() override completes, the global logging.disable level should be restored to its original value, so subsequent tests are unaffected.
When logging.disable() was never called (or set to NOTSET), caplog.set_level() should behave identically to its previous behavior with no additional side effects.
